title: Transport, Communication and Industrial Development
syllabus: WAEC Geography, Regional Geography of Nigeria: transportation; communication; industry. Part B: transportation, industry
NERDC-based schemes: Transportation; Industry; Transport and communication in Nigeria; Manufacturing industries in Nigeria
objectives: describe the main modes of transport in Nigeria and their advantages and problems;
identify major seaports, airports and railway lines;
explain the importance of communication networks;
explain the factors that influence the location of industries;
describe Nigeria's main industrial centres and the problems of industrial development.
intro: Transport moves people and goods; communication moves information. Both are essential for trade and industry. In this lesson you will see how Nigeria's transport and communication networks developed, where industries are located and why, and what holds industrial growth back.

blocks.text: Road transport carries most of Nigeria's passengers and freight. The government has invested in new **standard-gauge railways**: Abuja–Kaduna (opened in July 2016), Warri–Itakpe (inaugurated in September 2020) and Lagos–Ibadan (inaugurated in June 2021). The older colonial-era main lines run from Lagos to Kano and Nguru and from Port Harcourt to Maiduguri.

items: **Seaports**: Lagos (Apapa and Tin Can Island), Onne and Port Harcourt, Warri and Calabar. The **Lekki Deep Sea Port**, opened in January 2023, can handle much larger ships and aims to reduce congestion at the older Lagos ports.
**International airports**: Murtala Muhammed (Lagos), Nnamdi Azikiwe (Abuja), Mallam Aminu Kano (Kano) and Port Harcourt.
**Inland waterways**: the Niger and Benue can carry barges and boats, but navigation depends on the season and dredging.
**Pipelines**: carry crude oil, gas and petroleum products between oilfields, refineries, depots and power stations.

blocks.text: **Communication** is the transfer of information from one place to another. Modern Nigeria relies on **telecommunications** — mobile phones, the internet and data networks — alongside radio, television, newspapers and postal services. Mobile telephony expanded rapidly after GSM licences were issued in 2001, and mobile phones are now used for calls, banking, trade and learning.

items: **Importance**: links businesses with customers and suppliers, supports banking and e-commerce, spreads news and education, helps emergency services and government administration.
**Problems**: uneven coverage in rural areas, cost of data, power supply problems for network equipment, vandalism of cables and masts.

blocks.text: **Industry** can be grouped into **primary** (extracting raw materials: farming, mining, fishing, forestry), **secondary** (manufacturing and processing), **tertiary** (services such as trade, transport and banking) and **quaternary** (information, research and technology).

items: **Raw materials**: heavy or perishable raw materials attract industry close to their source — cement works near limestone (Obajana, Ewekoro), refineries near oilfields.
**Market**: industries producing bulky or fragile goods (drinks, furniture) locate near large populations such as Lagos.
**Power**: reliable electricity is essential; many firms run their own generators.
**Labour**: availability of skilled and unskilled workers.
**Transport**: ports, roads and railways reduce costs — many industries cluster around the Lagos ports.
**Capital and government policy**: investment, incentives, export processing zones and free trade zones (e.g. the Lekki Free Trade Zone).

blocks.text: The privately owned **Dangote refinery** at Lekki was commissioned in May 2023 and began operations in January 2024. It is designed to refine about 650,000 barrels of crude oil per day — enough, its owners say, to meet Nigeria's domestic demand for fuel, which the country previously imported in large quantities.

items.title: Problems
items.text: Unreliable electricity; poor roads and port congestion; high cost of borrowing; competition from cheap imports; insecurity; multiple taxes and levies; shortage of some skilled workers.

items.title: Possible solutions
items.text: Improving power supply; investing in roads, rail and ports; access to credit for manufacturers; protecting and promoting local industries; improving security; training and technical education.

worked.title: Explaining an industrial location
worked.problem: Explain why a large cement factory was built at Obajana in Kogi State.
steps: Identify the main raw material: cement is made mainly from limestone, which is heavy and bulky.
Locate the raw material: there are large limestone deposits at Obajana.
Explain: building the factory at the source reduces the cost of transporting heavy raw materials; Kogi's central position also helps distribution to markets across Nigeria.

exam_tips: For each mode of transport, be ready to give advantages and problems with Nigerian examples.
When explaining industrial location, link the factor to the industry: e.g. cement — bulky raw material — located at the source.
Name specific ports, airports and railway lines; avoid general statements.

checks.q: Name Nigeria's three standard-gauge railway lines opened between 2016 and 2021.
Why do many industries locate in Lagos?
checks.a: Large market, seaports and airport, good access to imported raw materials, available labour, banks and services.

checks.q: Give two problems facing industries in Nigeria.
checks.a: Unreliable electricity and poor transport infrastructure (also competition from imports, insecurity, high cost of credit).

summary: Road carries most traffic; new standard-gauge railways link Abuja–Kaduna, Warri–Itakpe and Lagos–Ibadan; seaports, airports, inland waterways and pipelines complete the network.
The Lekki Deep Sea Port (2023) handles larger ships and aims to ease congestion at Apapa and Tin Can.
Telecommunications grew rapidly after 2001 and support business, banking and learning.

Industrial location depends on raw materials, market, power, labour, transport, capital and policy. Major centres include Lagos, Kano, Kaduna, Port Harcourt, Aba and Onitsha; power supply and infrastructure are the biggest constraints.

structured.q: (a) Name three modes of transport in Nigeria. (b) For each, give one advantage and one problem. (c) Suggest two ways of improving transport in Nigeria.
model: (a) Road, rail and water (air and pipeline are also accepted).

(b) Road — advantage: reaches most places and gives door-to-door service; problem: poor maintenance and congestion. Rail — advantage: cheap for bulky goods over long distances; problem: limited network and decayed old lines. Water — advantage: cheapest for bulky goods and links Nigeria to world trade; problem: seasonal navigation on rivers and port congestion.
(c) Regular maintenance and expansion of roads; extending the standard-gauge rail network; dredging rivers; developing new deep-sea ports such as Lekki and improving port efficiency.
points: (a) 3 marks; (b) 6 marks; (c) 6 marks (3 per suggestion, explained).

structured.q: Explain four factors that influence the location of industries in Nigeria, using examples.
model: 1. Raw materials: industries using heavy or bulky raw materials locate near them, e.g. cement at Obajana near limestone. 2. Market: industries producing bulky or perishable goods locate near large populations, e.g. food and drinks factories in Lagos. 3. Transport: access to ports and roads reduces costs, e.g. industries around Apapa. 4. Power: reliable electricity attracts industry; its absence raises costs. (Labour, capital and government policy, e.g. free trade zones, are also accepted.)
points: 3 marks for each factor: stated (1), explained (1), example (1).
